hypothesis: In measured stature-for-age data, the growth-velocity curves of boys and girls have closely similar shapes, but the girls' adolescent acceleration starts, peaks and ends earlier than the boys', and the two curves differ in amplitude.
pass_criterion: All three conditions hold. (1) Girls' age at peak height velocity (PHV) is earlier than boys' by at least 1.0 year, with the bootstrap 95% CI for the difference excluding 0. (2) The girls' velocity curve, shifted later by the estimated phase lag, correlates with the boys' curve at Pearson r >= 0.90 over ages 6-18. (3) The shift-aligned curves differ in peak amplitude, with the bootstrap 95% CI for the peak-velocity difference excluding 0. Condition (3) is the 'amplitude' part of the claim. The curves are survey-weighted NHANES mean stature by sex in 3-month age bins, smoothed with LOESS or a monotone spline and differenced to give cm/year. Peak ages and CIs come from 1000 bootstrap resamples of survey primary sampling units.
fail_criterion: Any one of the following refutes the claim. (a) The PHV age difference (boys minus girls) is below 0.5 years, or its 95% CI includes 0, or girls peak later. (b) The phase-aligned correlation is below 0.80, meaning the shapes are not similar. (c) The aligned peak amplitudes do not differ, with the CI of the difference including 0. Values between the pass and fail thresholds count as inconclusive.
interpretation: Thompson's 'curve of growth velocity' is the first derivative of stature with respect to age, in cm/year. His 'phase' is the timing of the adolescent acceleration, measured by onset age, PHV age and end age. His 'amplitude' is peak velocity. 'Similar curve' is operationalised as a high correlation after a pure time shift. Modern reinterpretation: Thompson used longitudinal series of individual or mean children. NHANES is cross-sectional, so velocity is inferred from the age-gradient of population mean stature. This blurs individual peaks because of the tempo variation between children, and it flattens and widens the peak. It biases amplitude downward in both sexes, so the amplitude comparison is only relative. Phase differences are still estimable. Secular trends are minimal over a short pooled period, but the pooled cycles should be restricted to a limited range, for example 2011-2020 (before the pandemic gap).

dataset.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), Body Measures (BMX) and Demographics (DEMO) data files
dataset.publisher: US CDC National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)
dataset.why_it_fits: NHANES records measured, not self-reported, standing height (BMX: BMXHT, cm) for children and adolescents. The Demographics file gives sex (RIAGENDR), age in years (RIDAGEYR) and exam age in months (RIDAGEEX). It also gives survey weights (WTMEC2YR) and the design variables SDMVPSU and SDMVSTRA. Files are downloadable as SAS transport (XPT) files. They can be pooled across cycles, so the 2-20 year age range has enough sample for sex-specific mean-stature-by-age curves, from which velocity, PHV age and amplitude can be derived.
